catalog_quote: 13.4. Tones. There is a system of lexically significant pitch shapes, or tones. An independent word, i.e. any word other than a suffix, an enclitic or a grammatical auxiliary, has one and only one contrastive tone. The number of morphemes within the word is not significant. The first tone is dominant in the entire phrase or immediate constituent of the clause in the sense that it imposes its characteristic pitch shape upon the whole sequence. The number of syllables in such an immediate constituent of the clause from the point of tone onset onwards is significant through control of the allophonics. 13.4.1. new_statements.quote: 13.4. Tones. There is a system of lexically significant pitch shapes, or tones. An independent word, i.e. any word other than a suffix, an enclitic or a grammatical auxiliary, has one and only one contrastive tone. The number of morphemes within the word is not significant. The first tone is dominant in the entire phrase or immediate constituent of the clause in the sense that it imposes its characteristic pitch shape upon the whole sequence. [...] 13.5. Intonation and accent. Intonational stresses and lengths are strikingly different from those of the standard in the following respects. Isolated syllables before pause are lengthened so as to assign the extra length not to the vowel but to the syllable final.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Ray (1966) analyses Chittagong Bengali as having lexical word-tone (rising / falling / level), exactly one contrastive tone per independent word regardless of morpheme count, with the first word's tone spreading over the phrase; stress and length are treated as intonational (pre-pausal syllables lengthened on the coda), and no position of word stress is given. The only positional statement found is older: Pargiter 1886 p. 68 (copied by Grierson 1903 LSI V-1 p. 293) says that in polysyllables, especially Perso-Arabic loans, 'the accent is thrown back as far as possible, and the following syllables are lightened' - i.e. retracted/initial accent with reduction of post-tonic syllables.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None mentioned in any source opened.
new_statements.exceptions: Ray: suffixes, enclitics and grammatical auxiliaries carry no tone of their own; tone realisation (glide on 1st vs 2nd syllable) depends on the number of syllables from tone onset. Pargiter/Grierson: the retraction is said to hold 'especially' for Persian/Arabic loans (examples haoyala > háola, elaka > élaka). Ray flags his whole Chittagong chapter as based on 'an inadequate sampling and an equally inadequate analysis' (p. 89).
new_statements.domain_note: Ray's tone is word-level (one per independent word) but phonetically phrase-dominant; his stress/length remarks are explicitly intonational (pre-pausal, phrase level). Pargiter's 'accent' is word-level, illustrated with citation forms of loanwords.
new_statements.identity_note: All three primary statements concern the Bengali of Chittagong District ('Chittagong dialect' / 'South-Eastern Bengali, Chatgaiya') = Glottolog chit1275 Chittagonian [ctg]. Grierson's South-Eastern group also covers Noakhali and Akyab (the latter ~ Rohingya rohi1238), but the accent sentence sits in the Chittagong District section and derives from Pargiter's Chittagong-town notes. Ray 1966 does not name a locality within Chittagong.

sources.note: pp. ~142-143: West Central Bengali stress 'predominantly initial'; 'The stress system in other dialects has not been properly studied; the general tendency now seems to be to bring it to the head of the word, but non-initial stress is still present in many forms of folk-Bengali.' Nothing specific to Chittagong accent (only notes Chittagong nasalisation from -m-).

sources.citation: Grierson, G. A. 1903. Linguistic Survey of India, Vol. V, Part I: Indo-Aryan Family, Eastern Group (Bengali and Assamese). Calcutta. 'South-Eastern Dialect (Chittagong District)', pronunciation pp. 292-293.
sources.note: p. 293 (page image saved): 'In words of several syllables, especially those borrowed from Persian or Arabic, the accent is thrown back as far as possible, and the following syllables are lightened. Thus haōyālā (Arabic), a charge, becomes hāolā, a kind of land tenure; ēlākā (Arabic), connexion, becomes ēlakā.' Grierson states the account 'is based on Mr. Pargiter's work' - i.e. second-hand from Pargiter 1886.

sources.citation: Pargiter, F. E. 1886. Notes on the Chittagong Dialect. Journal of the Asiatic Society of Bengal 55, Part I, No. 1, pp. 66 ff. (archive.org dli.bengal.10689.14192).
sources.note: p. 68, 'Corruption of Words' item (6): 'In words of several syllables, especially those borrowed from Persian and Arabic, the accent is thrown back as far as possible, and the following syllables are lightened; thus হওয়ালা (Arab. حواله) "charge" becomes হাওলা "a háola"...; এলাকা (Arab. علاقه) "connexion" becomes এলকা.' I.e. retracted (initial) accent with reduction of following syllables. Verified on the page image (PDF p. 77).
Phonology section lists consonants/vowels only; no mention of tone, stress or accent; cites Učida 1970 p. 8, Hai 1965, Moniruzzaman 2007.
